blocks.html: Load balancers are intermediary servers that enable horizontal scaling by sitting between clients and a cluster of backend servers, to evenly distribute incoming network traffic across multiple servers.
blocks.text: Load balancers are intermediary servers that enable horizontal scaling by sitting between clients and a cluster of backend servers, to evenly distribute incoming network traffic across multiple servers.

blocks.html: Placement of Load Balancers
blocks.text: Placement of Load Balancers

blocks.html: Load balancers can be added at each layer of the system.

blocks.html: Common placements include:

blocks.html: Between users (clients) and web servers.

blocks.html: Between web servers and internal service layers.

blocks.html: Between internal service layers and database servers.

blocks.html: Load Balancing Algorithms
blocks.text: Load Balancing Algorithms

blocks.html: Load balancers can also be seen as servers which run algorithms which try to evenly distribute the requests.
blocks.text: Load balancers can also be seen as servers which run algorithms which try to evenly distribute the requests.

blocks.html: Following are some of those algorithms:
blocks.text: Following are some of those algorithms:

blocks.html: Round Robin: Sequentially cycle over the servers as the requests come.
blocks.text: Round Robin: Sequentially cycle over the servers as the requests come.

blocks.html: Weighted Round Robin: An extension of Round Robin where each server is assigned a weight based on its processing capacity. Servers with higher weights get more requests.
blocks.text: Weighted Round Robin: An extension of Round Robin where each server is assigned a weight based on its processing capacity. Servers with higher weights get more requests.

blocks.html: Least Connection Method: This method directs traffic to the server with the fewest active connections. It is useful when there are many unevenly distributed persistent connections.
blocks.text: Least Connection Method: This method directs traffic to the server with the fewest active connections. It is useful when there are many unevenly distributed persistent connections.

blocks.html: Least Response Time Method: This directs traffic to the server with the fewest active connections and the lowest average response time.
blocks.text: Least Response Time Method: This directs traffic to the server with the fewest active connections and the lowest average response time.

blocks.html: Least Bandwidth Method: This method selects the server that is currently serving the least amount of traffic, measured in megabits per second (Mbps).
blocks.text: Least Bandwidth Method: This method selects the server that is currently serving the least amount of traffic, measured in megabits per second (Mbps).

blocks.html: IP Hash: Under this method, a hash of the client's IP address is calculated to determine which server receives the request.
blocks.text: IP Hash: Under this method, a hash of the client's IP address is calculated to determine which server receives the request.

blocks.html: The load balancer applies a hashing function (like MD5 or CRC) to the client’s IP address.
blocks.text: The load balancer applies a hashing function (like MD5 or CRC) to the client’s IP address.

blocks.html: The result of this hash is mapped to a specific backend server in the server pool.
blocks.text: The result of this hash is mapped to a specific backend server in the server pool.

blocks.html: This way requests from the same client IP always go to the same server, maintaining session consistency, required for stateful applications.
blocks.text: This way requests from the same client IP always go to the same server, maintaining session consistency, required for stateful applications.

blocks.html: Intelligent Load Balancers: These LBs can periodically query backend servers about their load and adjust traffic distribution based on that information.

blocks.html: Health Checks
blocks.text: Health Checks

blocks.html: Load balancers must forward traffic only to "healthy" backend servers to ensure reliability.
blocks.text: Load balancers must forward traffic only to "healthy" backend servers to ensure reliability.

blocks.html: To monitor the health of a server, LBs use health checks, which are regular connection attempts to ensure servers are listening and responding appropriately.
blocks.text: To monitor the health of a server, LBs use health checks, which are regular connection attempts to ensure servers are listening and responding appropriately.

blocks.html: If a server fails a health check, it is automatically removed from the pool of available servers.
blocks.text: If a server fails a health check, it is automatically removed from the pool of available servers.

blocks.html: The LB will stop sending traffic to an unhealthy server until it begins to respond to health checks again.
blocks.text: The LB will stop sending traffic to an unhealthy server until it begins to respond to health checks again.

blocks.html: Redundancy in Load Balancers
blocks.text: Redundancy in Load Balancers

blocks.html: A single load balancer can become a single point of failure. To ensure high availability, multiple load balancers can be deployed in two main configurations: Active-Passive and Active-Active.
blocks.text: A single load balancer can become a single point of failure. To ensure high availability, multiple load balancers can be deployed in two main configurations: Active-Passive and Active-Active.

blocks.html: Active-Passive Configuration
blocks.text: Active-Passive Configuration

blocks.html: One load balancer (active) handles all traffic.
blocks.text: One load balancer (active) handles all traffic.

blocks.html: The second load balancer (passive/standby) remains idle, ready to take over if the active fails.
blocks.text: The second load balancer (passive/standby) remains idle, ready to take over if the active fails.

blocks.html: How it works:
blocks.text: How it works:

blocks.html: Passive LB constantly monitors the active LB (health checks).
blocks.text: Passive LB constantly monitors the active LB (health checks).

blocks.html: If active LB fails, passive LB becomes active and starts handling traffic.
blocks.text: If active LB fails, passive LB becomes active and starts handling traffic.

blocks.html: Use cases:
blocks.text: Use cases:

blocks.html: Systems where traffic can be handled by a single LB.
blocks.text: Systems where traffic can be handled by a single LB.

blocks.html: Simpler setup with lower cost.
blocks.text: Simpler setup with lower cost.

blocks.html: Pros:
blocks.text: Pros:

blocks.html: Simpler to implement.
blocks.text: Simpler to implement.

blocks.html: Only one LB processes traffic, so no conflicts.
blocks.text: Only one LB processes traffic, so no conflicts.

blocks.html: Cons:
blocks.text: Cons:

blocks.html: Passive LB sits idle most of the time (resources underutilized).
blocks.text: Passive LB sits idle most of the time (resources underutilized).

blocks.html: Slight downtime during failover (depending on monitoring and failover mechanism).
blocks.text: Slight downtime during failover (depending on monitoring and failover mechanism).

blocks.html: Active-Active Configuration
blocks.text: Active-Active Configuration

blocks.html: Multiple load balancers are active simultaneously, sharing traffic load.
blocks.text: Multiple load balancers are active simultaneously, sharing traffic load.

blocks.html: How it works:
blocks.text: How it works:

blocks.html: Traffic is split between all active LBs.
blocks.text: Traffic is split between all active LBs.

blocks.html: Each LB monitors the others for health.
blocks.text: Each LB monitors the others for health.

blocks.html: If one fails, the remaining LBs continue to handle traffic.
blocks.text: If one fails, the remaining LBs continue to handle traffic.

blocks.html: Use cases:
blocks.text: Use cases:

blocks.html: High-traffic systems needing load distribution and zero downtime.
blocks.text: High-traffic systems needing load distribution and zero downtime.

blocks.html: Critical applications requiring both availability and performance.
blocks.text: Critical applications requiring both availability and performance.

blocks.html: Pros:
blocks.text: Pros:

blocks.html: No single point of failure.
blocks.text: No single point of failure.

blocks.html: Better resource utilization, as all LBs handle traffic.
blocks.text: Better resource utilization, as all LBs handle traffic.

blocks.html: Seamless failover; traffic continues without interruption.
blocks.text: Seamless failover; traffic continues without interruption.

blocks.html: Cons:
blocks.text: Cons:

blocks.html: More complex setup and configuration.
blocks.text: More complex setup and configuration.

blocks.html: Requires careful synchronization to avoid session inconsistencies (stateful apps).
blocks.text: Requires careful synchronization to avoid session inconsistencies (stateful apps).
